html_en:
OpenAI is having a moment — and the ripples are being felt everywhere from your phone's trip-planning app to the world's largest infrastructure buildout. Today's dispatch is about what it actually takes to make AI work, at every layer of the stack.

🚀 "It Just Worked": ChatGPT as Your Personal Chief of Staff

The most-liked post in today's feed wasn't from a pundit or an analyst. It was Sam Altman describing what he did from his phone:

"Use all my chat history to figure out ideas for a long weekend trip with 8 friends, plan the best three options, make a full-stack site where the 9 of us can coordinate on what we would want to do in each place and decide where to go, and then after we get to group agreement make reservations. Draft an email in my Gmail I can send out to my friends when the site is ready." It...just worked.
— @sama

That tweet — nearly 15,000 likes — captures something important: the shift from AI as a writing assistant to AI as an autonomous agent that touches your calendar, your Gmail, your friends' plans, and the open web in a single prompt. Altman added that "work" undersells it, and that he wants "a new kind of computer."

OpenAI insider @thsottiaux — posting from inside the company — echoed the mood: "Vibes are strong. Never seen OpenAI more focused and humming." And separately made the case for ambient utility:

"It does at least 20 things for me every single day and I'm still surprised."
— @thsottiaux

Meanwhile, Dan Shipper is taking the week off to write what he calls "the definitive history of how Codex happened," based on deep interviews with OpenAI insiders — worth watching for when it drops on Every.

⚡ The Infrastructure Beneath Everything: "Factories That Turn Electrons Into Tokens"

If the product layer is humming, the physical layer is roaring. OpenAI's Head of Industrial Compute, Sachin Katti, sat down with Matt Turck on the MAD Podcast to describe what building at this scale actually feels like. Watch/Listen: OpenAI's Compute Chief: We Can't Build Fast Enough

"Anytime you have thought you have enough compute, we can slow down — always negatively surprises. Demand far outstrips compute supply today. So anything we can bring online, we consume immediately."
— Sachin Katti

The numbers are staggering: roughly $50 billion in compute spend from OpenAI alone this year, against an industry-wide figure approaching $700 billion. Katti's framing of a data center is vivid and worth keeping:

"The best way to visualize data centers is giant factories that are turning electrons into tokens... Large football fields, liquid cooled, because these chips run really hot."
— Sachin Katti

The conversation also touched on something genuinely vertiginous: AI beginning to help design its own chips. As Katti put it, "we do believe that the world of recursion is not that far, where AI will design the systems it needs to train and run the next generation of AI."

🏗️ The Applied Layer: Where Intelligence Meets Reality

Better models don't automatically produce better outcomes in the real world — and Box CEO Aaron Levie made that case with rare clarity today:

"Intelligence alone is not enough to transform most processes because you need to bridge that intelligence with real world feedback loops. That requires connecting to various enterprise systems, getting the right data to the AI, enabling humans to make decisions at different steps in a process through the right UX... The way you implement AI agents for doing client onboarding in a bank is entirely different from contract review in a legal team."
— @levie

His counterintuitive kicker: the better models get, the more you need the applied layer, not less — because more capable AI enables more ambitious automation, which demands deeper integration. This cuts against the narrative that foundation model improvements will commoditize everything downstream.

@realmadhuguru offered a complementary framing: we're in Phase 1, where companies with distribution expand into adjacent features using AI as accelerant. Phase 2 — net-new innovation that reshapes the software ecosystem — is still coming.

🔓 Open Weights, Trust Gaps, and the Security Paradox

Guillermo Rauch announced that Vercel is co-signing the Open Weights and American AI Leadership letter, calling open weights "the logical next frontier" after open source, data, and protocols. The move signals that the developer-tools community is increasingly aligned with the open model movement on both principled and strategic grounds.

But there's a wrinkle. Amjad Masad flagged a notable data point from a former Anthropic employee:

"Hackers prefer to use massively subsidized labs AI subscriptions for attacks as opposed to open models."
— @amasad

The implication is uncomfortable: closed, subsidized models may be doing more harm-enabling than open ones, inverting much of the safety argument against open weights. And separately, Peter Yang noted that outside the AI-native bubble, mainstream users' number one concern isn't hallucinations or token limits — it's whether they trust ChatGPT enough to hand over their Gmail, Calendar, and Office accounts. Trust, not capability, remains the adoption bottleneck.

📐 Craft Notes: Metrics, Earnestness, and the Blank Box Problem

A handful of quieter observations from today's feed are worth sitting with. @zarazhangrui offered a sharp reframe on how to measure AI adoption: "Stop measuring your AI adoption in tokens burned. Measure the time from a user need arriving to that thing shipping." And on why AI tutorials proliferate: "the more general a chat product is, the harder it is to use. People face a blank box and freeze."

At YC Startup School 2026, Garry Tan closed with two words that could serve as a motto for the current moment: "Don't LARP. Be earnest." Sam Altman was the anchor speaker — by all accounts, a fitting close to a year when the gap between demo theater and genuine utility has never mattered more.
html_zh:
今天的AI世界有一个清晰的主线：从算力基础设施的史诗级扩张，到ChatGPT真正"替你干活"的现实落地，智能正在以惊人的速度从实验室走进日常生活——而这场变革才刚刚开始。

🏗️ 史上最大基础设施建设：OpenAI的算力野心

如果你想理解AI竞赛的底层逻辑，不妨听听OpenAI工业算力负责人 Sachin Katti 的描述。在接受 The MAD Podcast 采访时，这位前Intel CTO、斯坦福教授用一句话概括了他每天的工作状态：

"需求的饥渴程度远超算力供给。我们能上线的任何算力，都会被立刻消化掉。"

OpenAI今年的算力支出预计约为500亿美元，整个行业的算力投入则可能高达7000亿美元。Katti将这些数据中心描述为"将电子转化为tokens的巨型工厂"——成排的液冷超级计算机，连电缆和变压器都需要冷却，因为"任何处理能量的东西都会产生热量"。

更令人深思的是他对未来的预判：

"我们相信，AI自己设计下一代AI所需系统的递归时代已经不远了。"

Watch/Listen: OpenAI's Compute Chief: We Can't Build Fast Enough | Sachin Katti

📱 "帮我干活"：ChatGPT的代理时代真的来了

理论归理论，但这一周最让AI圈沸腾的，是 Sam Altman 随手发出的一条推文。他用手机发了一段指令：

"用我所有的聊天记录，帮我找8个朋友长周末出行的想法，规划最佳的三个选项，做一个全栈网站让9个人一起协调、投票决定去哪，达成共识后帮我订好，再在我的Gmail里起草一封邮件，等网站好了发给朋友们。"
——然后，它就真的做到了。

这条推文获得了近1.5万个点赞。OpenAI内部人士 @thsottiaux 也在推波助澜：

"让ChatGPT替你工作。谈判宽带账单、清理垃圾订阅邮件、找到最划算的交易……真的就是一句提示词的事。它每天至少帮我做20件事，我到现在还会感到惊讶。"

与此同时，@thsottiaux 也分享了一个难得的内部观感："气氛非常对。我从未见过OpenAI如此专注、如此高效运转。"

🏢 "应用层"才是真正的战场

模型越来越强，但 Aaron Levie（Box CEO）提出了一个清醒的观点：光有智能还不够。

"在银行做客户入职的AI Agent，和法律团队做合同审查的AI Agent，实现方式完全不同。在生命科学、金融服务、法律、制造业这些关键行业，AI只有以有针对性的方式接触真实世界，才有价值。这种接触需要一个'应用层'来实现。"

更有反直觉的洞察：模型越强，对应用层的需求反而越大——因为你能想象去自动化的工作流程变得更加宏大，需要更深度的系统集成。这对独立的垂直AI公司来说是个巨大的机会。

@realmadhuguru 则给那些说"AI没有产品影响"的人泼了一盆冷水：

"现在是第一阶段。有分发渠道的公司正在快速扩张到邻近的问题领域——AI帮助他们快速执行，构建以前需要大量定制软件才能实现的功能。第二阶段将会出现更多净新功能和创新，那时AI对软件生态的影响将无可辩驳。"

🔓 开放权重、信任危机与安全隐患

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch 高调宣布联署"开放权重与美国AI领导力"倡议书：

"开源、数据、协议和研究成就了我们今天享有的技术奇迹。开放权重是合乎逻辑的下一个前沿。"

但开放带来便利，也带来风险。Amjad Masad（Replit CEO）转发了一项前Anthropic员工的披露：

"黑客更倾向于使用受大量补贴的商业AI订阅服务发动攻击，而非使用开源模型。"

这是一个讽刺性的悖论：正是那些为了普及AI而压低价格的实验室，也在无意中降低了恶意行为者的成本门槛。

在普通用户层面，@petergyang 从加拿大带回了一线用户的真实顾虑：

"现在和没有'AI焦虑'的普通人聊天，他们最担心的不是token用完，而是'我能不能信任ChatGPT来共享我的Gmail、日历、Google Workspace？'"

AI Agent时代的最大摩擦力，或许不是技术能力，而是用户信任。

💡 今日金句

最后，几句值得收藏的碎片智慧——

Garry Tan（YC总裁）在Startup School闭幕时留下了最简洁的创业箴言：

"不要扮演，要真诚。"

@zarazhangrui 给了一个更犀利的产品度量建议：

"别再用消耗了多少token来衡量AI采用率。去量从用户需求出现到功能上线的时间。"

而 Dan Shipper（Every）则宣布将休假一周，完成一篇"OpenAI Codex诞生史"的深度报道——凭借内部人士深度采访写成，值得期待。
